139	## Appendix: SaaS Metrics Reference
140	
141	Canonical formulas and thresholds for SaaS-specific metrics referenced in evaluations. Use these definitions exactly — do not improvise alternative formulas.
142	
143	**If required inputs for a metric are not available from the startup's materials, state this explicitly — do not estimate or assume values.**
144	
145	| Metric | Formula | Key Thresholds | Stage Relevance |
146	|--------|---------|---------------|-----------------|
147	| Magic Number | `(Qtr Rev - Prev Qtr Rev) * 4 / Prev Qtr S&M` | >1.0 efficient, 0.5–1.0 moderate, <0.5 inefficient | Meaningful at Series A with quarterly revenue data. Pre-seed/seed: rarely available, do not require. |
148	| Burn Multiple | `Net Burn / Net New ARR` | <1.5x good, 1.5–2.0x acceptable early, >3.0x red flag | Useful at seed with ARR trajectory. Pre-seed: typically N/A (no ARR). |
149	| Rule of 40 | `Rev Growth % + Profit Margin %` | >40% strong, 20–40% acceptable early, <20% concerning | Series A and later. Pre-seed/seed: growth should dominate; margin is secondary. Note: some firms use "Rule of X" (`Growth % × 2 + FCF Margin %`) which weights growth more heavily — do not substitute without stating which variant is used. |
150	| CAC | `Total S&M / New Customers` | Varies by ACV; break down by channel at Series A | Seed: blended CAC is useful. Series A: channel-level CAC expected. Pre-seed: too early. |
151	| New CAC Ratio | `S&M / New Customer ARR` | <$1.50 good, $1.50–$2.00 acceptable, >$2.00 expensive (2025 median $2.00) | Series A+. Isolates pure acquisition cost from expansion revenue. Use alongside Blended CAC Ratio. |
152	| Blended CAC Ratio | `S&M / (New Customer ARR + Expansion ARR)` | Lower is better; compare to New CAC Ratio to see expansion leverage | Series A+. Shows how expansion revenue amortizes acquisition cost. |
153	| LTV/CAC | `(ARPA × Gross Margin / Churn) / CAC` | >3.0x healthy, <1.0x unsustainable | Seed: directional estimate acceptable. Series A: must be computed with real data. Pre-seed: N/A. |
154	| NDR (Net Dollar Retention) | `(Beg ARR + Expansion - Contraction - Churn) / Beg ARR` | >130% elite, 110–130% good, <100% concerning | Meaningful at seed with 6+ months of cohort data. Series A: expected. Pre-seed: N/A. Always pair with GRR — high NDR can mask high base churn if expansion from a few large accounts dominates. |
155	| GRR (Gross Revenue Retention) | `(Beg ARR - Churn - Contraction) / Beg ARR` | >95% elite, 90–95% strong, 85–90% acceptable, <85% concerning | Same as NDR: meaningful at seed with 6+ months of cohort data. Series A: expected alongside NDR. Pre-seed: N/A. Shows the "leaky bucket" baseline — churn and contraction only, no expansion. |
156	| CAC Payback | `CAC / (ARPA × Gross Margin)` | <12mo excellent, 12–18mo good, >24mo concerning (enterprise ACV may tolerate up to 24mo due to high LTV and low churn) | Seed: useful if data available. Series A: expected. Pre-seed: too early. |
157	| ARR per Employee | `Total ARR / Headcount` | >$150K good early-stage, $200K–$300K+ at scale (AI-native companies often 4–5× higher) | Seed onward as a capital-efficiency signal. Pre-seed: team too small for this to be meaningful. |
158	| Gross Margin | (cross-ref `biz_gross_margins` dimension) | SaaS >70% (top-tier >75%), marketplace >60%, services >40%. AI-native companies may run 25–60% due to inference/infra costs — flag but do not penalize if acknowledged with a path to improvement. | All stages. Pre-seed: target margins acceptable. Seed+: actual margins expected. |
159	
160	---
161	
162	## Appendix: Concern vs. Dealbreaker Thresholds
163	
164	When evaluating a dimension, the boundary between `concern` and `dealbreaker` determines whether the startup gets a "work on this" signal or a hard pass. The following guidance covers the highest-impact dimensions per category.
165	
166	**General rule:** When uncertain, default to `concern`. A dealbreaker is a finding so severe that no amount of strength in other areas can compensate — it makes the investment fundamentally unworkable.
167	
168	| Category | Dimension | Dealbreaker if... |
169	|----------|-----------|-------------------|
170	| **Team** | `team_founder_market_fit` | Founders have zero relevant domain experience AND cannot articulate a credible "why me" — no lived experience, no unfair insight, no relevant network. |
171	| **Team** | `team_coachability` | Founders are actively hostile to feedback or have a documented pattern of ignoring advisor/investor input across multiple interactions. |
172	| **Market** | `market_size_credibility` | The addressable market is provably too small for fund-returning outcomes (e.g., niche with <$100M SAM and no plausible expansion path). |
173	| **Product** | `product_traction_evidence` | At seed+: zero paying customers AND no credible pipeline (LOIs, pilots, waitlist) after 6+ months of effort. Pre-seed: this dimension is rarely a dealbreaker. |
174	| **Business Model** | `biz_unit_economics` | At Series A: unit economics are negative with no improvement trend AND the business model has no structural path to positive unit economics. |
175	| **Financials** | `fin_runway_plan` | Runway is <6 months with no funding pipeline and milestones are unachievable within remaining capital. |
176	| **Risk** | `risk_single_point_failure` | Business depends entirely on a single customer (>80% revenue), single platform (no migration path), or single regulation that is actively under threat. |
177	| **Risk** | `risk_regulatory` | The core business activity is illegal in key target markets or faces imminent regulatory prohibition with no pivot path. |
178	| **Fund Fit** | `fit_portfolio_conflict` | Direct, blocking portfolio conflict — the fund already has an investment in a direct competitor in the same market segment. |

13	| `concern` | Weakness identified. Partners would raise this in discussion. | 0.0 |
14	| `dealbreaker` | Fatal flaw. Any single dealbreaker forces a `hard_pass` verdict. | 0.0 (forces hard_pass) |
15	| `not_applicable` | Dimension doesn't apply to this company's stage or model. | excluded |
16	
17	## Scoring Formula
18	
19	```
20	applicable = count of items where status != "not_applicable"
21	conviction_score = (strong*1.0 + moderate*0.5) / applicable * 100
22	```
23	
24	### Verdicts
25	
26	| Score Range | Verdict | Meaning |
27	|-------------|---------|---------|
28	| >= 75% | `invest` | Strong enough for a term sheet discussion |
29	| >= 50% | `more_diligence` | Promising but needs more evidence on key dimensions |
30	| < 50% | `pass` | Too many concerns to proceed at this time |
31	| any dealbreaker | `hard_pass` | Fatal flaw identified — cannot proceed regardless of score |
32	
33	### Zero-Applicable Edge Case
34	
35	If all 28 dimensions are marked `not_applicable` (or no items provided), the score is `0.0` and the verdict is `more_diligence` with a `ZERO_APPLICABLE_DIMENSIONS` warning. This prevents false positives from empty evaluations.
36	
37	## Categories and Dimensions
38	
39	### Team (4 dimensions)
40	
41	| ID | Dimension | Description |
42	|----|-----------|-------------|
43	| `team_founder_market_fit` | Founder-Market Fit | Do the founders have unique insight, domain expertise, or unfair advantage in this market? Have they lived the problem they're solving? |
44	| `team_complementary_skills` | Complementary Skills | Does the founding team cover the critical bases (technical, commercial, domain)? Are there obvious gaps that need to be filled? |
45	| `team_execution_speed` | Execution Speed | Is the team shipping fast relative to their resources? Evidence of rapid iteration, quick pivots, and bias toward action. |
46	| `team_coachability` | Coachability | Does the founding team take feedback well? Evidence of adapting based on customer/investor/advisor input. Defensiveness is a red flag. |
47	
48	**Stage calibration:**
49	- **Pre-seed:** Founder-market fit and coachability matter most. Team gaps are expected and acceptable.
50	- **Seed:** Complementary skills become important. Solo founders need a plan to build the team.
51	- **Series A:** Full team evaluation. Execution speed must be demonstrated, not just claimed.
52	
53	### Market (4 dimensions)
54	
55	| ID | Dimension | Description |
56	|----|-----------|-------------|
57	| `market_size_credibility` | Size Credibility | Is the stated market size credible and well-sourced? Bottom-up > top-down. Segment-specific > total industry. |
58	| `market_timing` | Timing | Is there a clear macro catalyst (regulatory, technological, behavioral) that makes now the right time? |
59	| `market_growth_trajectory` | Growth Trajectory | Is the market growing, stable, or shrinking? What's the CAGR? Are tailwinds accelerating? |
60	| `market_entry_barriers` | Entry Barriers | How hard is it for new competitors to enter? Regulatory barriers, network effects, switching costs, or technical complexity. |
61	
62	**Stage calibration:**
63	- **Pre-seed:** Market insight matters more than precise sizing. A compelling "why now" can compensate for loose TAM.
64	- **Seed:** Market size should be bottom-up sourced. Timing argument should be concrete.
65	- **Series A:** Market must be large enough for fund-returning outcomes. Growth trajectory must be validated with data.
66	
67	### Product (4 dimensions)
68	
69	| ID | Dimension | Description |
70	|----|-----------|-------------|
71	| `product_differentiation` | Differentiation | What makes this product meaningfully different from alternatives? Feature parity is not differentiation. |
72	| `product_traction_evidence` | Traction Evidence | Concrete proof of product-market fit: revenue, users, engagement metrics, LOIs, waitlist size. Stage-appropriate. |
73	| `product_technical_moat` | Technical Moat | Is there something technically difficult to replicate? Proprietary data, unique architecture, patents, or deep domain-specific engineering. |
74	| `product_user_love` | User Love | Do users/customers actively love the product? NPS, unsolicited referrals, retention data, customer quotes. |
75	
76	**Stage calibration:**
77	- **Pre-seed:** Differentiation and early signal (waitlist, LOIs) suffice. Technical moat can be a plan.
78	- **Seed:** Traction evidence must be concrete (paying customers). User love should be demonstrable.
79	- **Series A:** All four dimensions should show strength. Technical moat must be built, not planned.
80	
81	### Business Model (4 dimensions)
82	
83	| ID | Dimension | Description |
84	|----|-----------|-------------|
85	| `biz_unit_economics` | Unit Economics | Are per-unit economics positive or trending positive? LTV/CAC, contribution margin, payback period. |
86	| `biz_pricing_power` | Pricing Power | Can the company raise prices without losing customers? Evidence of value-based pricing vs. cost-plus. |
87	| `biz_scalability` | Scalability | Does the business model scale without proportional cost increases? Marginal cost of serving the next customer. |
88	| `biz_gross_margins` | Gross Margins | Are gross margins appropriate for the business type? Software: >70%. Services: >40%. Hardware: >30%. |
89	
90	**Stage calibration:**
91	- **Pre-seed:** Business model hypothesis is sufficient. Pricing experiments are a plus.
92	- **Seed:** Unit economics should be emerging. Pricing should be tested with real customers.
93	- **Series A:** Unit economics must be proven and improving. Gross margins should be at or approaching target.
94	
95	### Financials (4 dimensions)
96	
97	| ID | Dimension | Description |
98	|----|-----------|-------------|
99	| `fin_capital_efficiency` | Capital Efficiency | How much value is created per dollar spent? Revenue per dollar raised, headcount efficiency. |
100	| `fin_runway_plan` | Runway Plan | Does current/planned funding provide enough runway to hit milestones for the next round? |
101	| `fin_path_to_next_round` | Path to Next Round | Are the milestones for the next funding round clearly defined and achievable within the runway? |
102	| `fin_revenue_quality` | Revenue Quality | Is revenue recurring, predictable, and diversified? Or lumpy, one-time, and concentrated? |
103	
104	**Stage calibration:**
105	- **Pre-seed:** Capital efficiency is about burn rate discipline. Revenue quality is N/A.
106	- **Seed:** Runway plan should cover 18-24 months. Revenue quality should be emerging.
107	- **Series A:** All financial dimensions should be well-evidenced. Revenue quality is critical.
108	
109	### Risk (4 dimensions)
110	
111	| ID | Dimension | Description |
112	|----|-----------|-------------|
113	| `risk_single_point_failure` | Single Point of Failure | Is the business dependent on one customer, one supplier, one platform, one regulation, or one person? |
114	| `risk_regulatory` | Regulatory Risk | Is the business exposed to regulatory change? How well-prepared is the team for regulatory shifts? |
115	| `risk_competitive_response` | Competitive Response | What happens when incumbents or well-funded startups respond? How defensible is the position? |
116	| `risk_customer_concentration` | Customer Concentration | Is revenue diversified across customers? Top customer <20% of revenue at seed, <10% at Series A. |
117	
118	**Stage calibration:**
119	- **Pre-seed:** Some concentration is expected. Key risk: founder dependency (no team backup).
120	- **Seed:** Concentration should be decreasing. Regulatory awareness should be evident.
121	- **Series A:** No single point of failure should remain unaddressed. Customer diversification is expected.
122	
123	### Fund Fit (4 dimensions)
124	
125	| ID | Dimension | Description |
126	|----|-----------|-------------|
127	| `fit_thesis_alignment` | Thesis Alignment | Does this investment align with the fund's stated investment thesis and focus areas? |
128	| `fit_portfolio_conflict` | Portfolio Conflict | Does the fund already have a conflicting investment? Direct overlap, customer overlap, or adjacent market. |
129	| `fit_stage_match` | Stage Match | Is this company at the right stage for the fund's typical investment? Check size, ownership targets, support model. |
130	| `fit_value_add` | Value-Add Potential | Can the fund add meaningful value beyond capital? Relevant portfolio companies, domain expertise, key relationships. |
131	
132	**Stage calibration:**
133	- Applies equally across all stages
134	- In generic mode: evaluate against a hypothetical early-stage fund thesis
135	- In fund-specific mode: evaluate against the researched fund's actual thesis, portfolio, and focus
136

138	
139	## Appendix: SaaS Metrics Reference
140	
141	Canonical formulas and thresholds for SaaS-specific metrics referenced in evaluations. Use these definitions exactly — do not improvise alternative formulas.
142	
143	**If required inputs for a metric are not available from the startup's materials, state this explicitly — do not estimate or assume values.**
144	
145	| Metric | Formula | Key Thresholds | Stage Relevance |
146	|--------|---------|---------------|-----------------|
147	| Magic Number | `(Qtr Rev - Prev Qtr Rev) * 4 / Prev Qtr S&M` | >1.0 efficient, 0.5–1.0 moderate, <0.5 inefficient | Meaningful at Series A with quarterly revenue data. Pre-seed/seed: rarely available, do not require. |
148	| Burn Multiple | `Net Burn / Net New ARR` | <1.5x good, 1.5–2.0x acceptable early, >3.0x red flag | Useful at seed with ARR trajectory. Pre-seed: typically N/A (no ARR). |
149	| Rule of 40 | `Rev Growth % + Profit Margin %` | >40% strong, 20–40% acceptable early, <20% concerning | Series A and later. Pre-seed/seed: growth should dominate; margin is secondary. Note: some firms use "Rule of X" (`Growth % × 2 + FCF Margin %`) which weights growth more heavily — do not substitute without stating which variant is used. |
150	| CAC | `Total S&M / New Customers` | Varies by ACV; break down by channel at Series A | Seed: blended CAC is useful. Series A: channel-level CAC expected. Pre-seed: too early. |
151	| New CAC Ratio | `S&M / New Customer ARR` | <$1.50 good, $1.50–$2.00 acceptable, >$2.00 expensive (2025 median $2.00) | Series A+. Isolates pure acquisition cost from expansion revenue. Use alongside Blended CAC Ratio. |
152	| Blended CAC Ratio | `S&M / (New Customer ARR + Expansion ARR)` | Lower is better; compare to New CAC Ratio to see expansion leverage | Series A+. Shows how expansion revenue amortizes acquisition cost. |
153	| LTV/CAC | `(ARPA × Gross Margin / Churn) / CAC` | >3.0x healthy, <1.0x unsustainable | Seed: directional estimate acceptable. Series A: must be computed with real data. Pre-seed: N/A. |
154	| NDR (Net Dollar Retention) | `(Beg ARR + Expansion - Contraction - Churn) / Beg ARR` | >130% elite, 110–130% good, <100% concerning | Meaningful at seed with 6+ months of cohort data. Series A: expected. Pre-seed: N/A. Always pair with GRR — high NDR can mask high base churn if expansion from a few large accounts dominates. |
155	| GRR (Gross Revenue Retention) | `(Beg ARR - Churn - Contraction) / Beg ARR` | >95% elite, 90–95% strong, 85–90% acceptable, <85% concerning | Same as NDR: meaningful at seed with 6+ months of cohort data. Series A: expected alongside NDR. Pre-seed: N/A. Shows the "leaky bucket" baseline — churn and contraction only, no expansion. |
156	| CAC Payback | `CAC / (ARPA × Gross Margin)` | <12mo excellent, 12–18mo good, >24mo concerning (enterprise ACV may tolerate up to 24mo due to high LTV and low churn) | Seed: useful if data available. Series A: expected. Pre-seed: too early. |
157	| ARR per Employee | `Total ARR / Headcount` | >$150K good early-stage, $200K–$300K+ at scale (AI-native companies often 4–5× higher) | Seed onward as a capital-efficiency signal. Pre-seed: team too small for this to be meaningful. |
158	| Gross Margin | (cross-ref `biz_gross_margins` dimension) | SaaS >70% (top-tier >75%), marketplace >60%, services >40%. AI-native companies may run 25–60% due to inference/infra costs — flag but do not penalize if acknowledged with a path to improvement. | All stages. Pre-seed: target margins acceptable. Seed+: actual margins expected. |
159

161	
162	## Appendix: Concern vs. Dealbreaker Thresholds
163	
164	When evaluating a dimension, the boundary between `concern` and `dealbreaker` determines whether the startup gets a "work on this" signal or a hard pass. The following guidance covers the highest-impact dimensions per category.
165	
166	**General rule:** When uncertain, default to `concern`. A dealbreaker is a finding so severe that no amount of strength in other areas can compensate — it makes the investment fundamentally unworkable.
167	
168	| Category | Dimension | Dealbreaker if... |
169	|----------|-----------|-------------------|
170	| **Team** | `team_founder_market_fit` | Founders have zero relevant domain experience AND cannot articulate a credible "why me" — no lived experience, no unfair insight, no relevant network. |
171	| **Team** | `team_coachability` | Founders are actively hostile to feedback or have a documented pattern of ignoring advisor/investor input across multiple interactions. |
172	| **Market** | `market_size_credibility` | The addressable market is provably too small for fund-returning outcomes (e.g., niche with <$100M SAM and no plausible expansion path). |
173	| **Product** | `product_traction_evidence` | At seed+: zero paying customers AND no credible pipeline (LOIs, pilots, waitlist) after 6+ months of effort. Pre-seed: this dimension is rarely a dealbreaker. |
174	| **Business Model** | `biz_unit_economics` | At Series A: unit economics are negative with no improvement trend AND the business model has no structural path to positive unit economics. |
175	| **Financials** | `fin_runway_plan` | Runway is <6 months with no funding pipeline and milestones are unachievable within remaining capital. |
176	| **Risk** | `risk_single_point_failure` | Business depends entirely on a single customer (>80% revenue), single platform (no migration path), or single regulation that is actively under threat. |
177	| **Risk** | `risk_regulatory` | The core business activity is illegal in key target markets or faces imminent regulatory prohibition with no pivot path. |
178	| **Fund Fit** | `fit_portfolio_conflict` | Direct, blocking portfolio conflict — the fund already has an investment in a direct competitor in the same market segment. |

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_019dyoJnLi2J2f8k4mh5TdqX","type":"tool_result","content":"1	# Partner Archetypes
2	
3	Three canonical partner archetypes for the IC simulation. Each archetype represents a real lens that VC partners bring to investment decisions. In a real fund, partners naturally gravitate toward one of these perspectives based on their background and experience.
4	
5	When running in **fund-specific mode**, map real partners to these archetypes based on their known focus areas and backgrounds. When running in **generic mode**, use the archetypes directly.
6	
7	## The Visionary
8	
9	**Background archetype:** Former founder, product leader, or market analyst. Thinks in decades and categories. Gets excited about timing and market creation.
10	
11	**Focus areas:**
12	- Market size and growth trajectory — not just current TAM but where the market is heading
13	- Timing — why this is the right moment (regulatory shifts, technology inflection points, behavioral changes)
14	- Category creation potential — is this defining a new category or competing in an existing one?
15	- 10-year vision — what does this company look like at scale? Does the founder think big enough?
16	- Network effects and compounding advantages — what gets better as the company grows?
17	
18	**Typical questions:**
19	- "What's the macro catalyst that makes this possible now and not five years ago?"
20	- "If this works, how big can it get? What's the ceiling?"
21	- "Who are the incumbents and why can't they do this?"
22	- "Is this a feature, a product, or a company?"
23	- "What does the world look like in 10 years if this company succeeds?"
24	- "Is this a $100M outcome or a $1B+ outcome?"
25	
26	**Conviction signals (what makes this partner say "invest"):**
27	- Founder has a unique insight about where the market is going
28	- Clear macro tailwind (regulatory, technology, demographic)
29	- Large and growing market with room for a new category leader
30	- Product vision that compounds — each new user/customer makes the product better
31	- Founder thinks about the business in terms of decades, not quarters
32	
33	**Red flags (what makes this partner say "pass"):**
34	- Small or shrinking market with no clear expansion path
35	- "Me too" product in a crowded space — no differentiation
36	- Founder can't articulate why now — feels like this could have been built anytime
37	- Vision is incremental — just a better version of what exists, not a new paradigm
38	- Market timing feels too early (no demand yet) or too late (incumbents entrenched)
39	
40	**Debate style:**
41	- Starts with the big picture, zooms in on specifics only when challenged
42	- Gets enthusiastic about narratives and analogies ("This is the Shopify of X")
43	- May overlook execution details in favor of market potential
44	- Can be persuaded by a compelling vision even when current metrics are weak
45	- Tends to disagree with The Analyst on what matters: "The TAM is huge, the current unit economics are fixable"
46	
47	## The Operator
48	
49	**Background archetype:** Former operating executive, GTM leader, or serial founder. Evaluates based on execution evidence and operational reality. Trusts data over narratives.
50	
51	**Focus areas:**
52	- Execution speed — how fast is the team shipping and iterating?
53	- GTM motion — is there a clear, repeatable path to acquiring customers?
54	- Competitive moat — what's defensible beyond "we're first"?
55	- Customer evidence — who is actually paying and why? What do churned customers say?
56	- Team composition — does the founding team have the skills needed for the next 2 years?
57	- Operational efficiency — how much value are they creating per dollar spent?
58	
59	**Typical questions:**
60	- "Walk me through how you acquire a customer. What's the playbook?"
61	- "What does your best customer say about you? What does your most recent churned customer say?"
62	- "Who are your next 3 hires and why those roles?"
63	- "What's your burn rate and what milestones does your runway cover?"
64	- "If I gave you double the money, what would you do differently?"
65	- "What's the hardest thing about your business that an outsider wouldn't understand?"
66	
67	**Conviction signals (what makes this partner say "invest"):**
68	- Clear evidence of product-market fit: customers actively pulling the product
69	- Repeatable customer acquisition channel with measurable economics
70	- Founder has deep operational expertise in the problem domain
71	- Team has complementary skills (technical + commercial)
72	- Speed of iteration is visibly fast — shipping weekly, learning from every customer
73	- Capital-efficient growth — doing more with less
74	
75	**Red flags (what makes this partner say "pass"):**
76	- No paying customers or only "design partners" with no clear conversion path
77	- Vague GTM: "We'll do content marketing and partnerships" with no specifics
78	- Solo technical founder with no commercial co-founder (for B2B)
79	- Burn rate suggests undisciplined spending (e.g., hired 20 people before product-market fit)
80	- Can't answer "why did your last customer churn?" — indicates lack of customer intimacy
81	- Execution speed is slow relative to competitors
82	
83	**Debate style:**
84	- Asks for specifics when others speak in generalities
85	- Pushes back on market-size arguments with "that's the TAM, what's the realistic SOM?"
86	- Values founder authenticity — respects "I don't know yet" more than a polished non-answer
87	- May dismiss a large market if the GTM motion isn't clear
88	- Tends to disagree with The Visionary: "The market is big, but can THIS team actually capture it?"
89	
90	## The Analyst
91	
92	**Background archetype:** Former investment banker, management consultant, or financial analyst. Evaluates based on numbers, financial models, and risk-adjusted returns. Trusts spreadsheets over stories.
93	
94	**Focus areas:**
95	- Unit economics — LTV/CAC, gross margins, contribution margin, payback period
96	- Burn rate and runway — how long can the company survive, what milestones does the money cover?
97	- Capital efficiency — revenue per dollar raised, headcount efficiency
98	- Cohort data — retention curves, expansion revenue, net dollar retention
99	- Financial modeling — path to profitability, scenario analysis, sensitivity to key assumptions
100	- Risk quantification — regulatory risk, concentration risk, competitive response timing
101	
102	**Typical questions:**
103	- "What are your fully-loaded unit economics? Include all variable costs."
104	- "Show me the cohort retention curves. What happens after month 6?"
105	- "What's your path to gross margin positive on a per-unit basis?"
106	- "If your top customer churns tomorrow, what happens to your metrics?"
107	- "What's the realistic path to your next funding round? What metrics do you need to hit?"
108	- "What's your customer concentration? Top 10 customers as percentage of revenue?"
109	
110	**Conviction signals (what makes this partner say "invest"):**
111	- Clean, improving unit economics — LTV/CAC > 3x, payback < 18 months
112	- Strong retention: net dollar retention > 100%, healthy cohort curves
113	- Capital-efficient business: growing revenue faster than headcount
114	- Clear financial model with realistic assumptions and identified risks
115	- Path to profitability that doesn't require heroic assumptions
116	- Revenue quality: recurring, predictable, diversified customer base
117	
118	**Red flags (what makes this partner say "pass"):**
119	- Negative or unclear unit economics with no credible path to improvement
120	- Customer concentration: >30% of revenue from a single customer
121	- Burn rate inconsistent with traction (spending $500K/month with $10K MRR)
122	- "Hockey stick" projections with no basis in current growth rate
123	- Founder can't explain their own financial model or gets defensive about numbers
124	- Round is overpriced relative to traction and comparable companies
125	
126	**Debate style:**
127	- Brings data to every argument — "The median Series A has X metrics, this company has Y"
128	- Challenges optimistic assumptions with sensitivity analysis
129	- Asks "what has to be true" for the investment thesis to work
130	- May be swayed by strong unit economics even in a market they find unexciting
131	- Tends to disagree with both partners: "The vision is compelling AND the GTM looks good, but the numbers say this is a $50M outcome, not $500M"
132	- Often the last to commit — wants to see the full picture before forming a view
133	
134	## Using Archetypes in the Simulation
135	
136	### Generic Mode
137	Use the archetypes directly. Name them "The Visionary," "The Operator," and "The Analyst." Each evaluates the startup through their distinctive lens.
138	
139	### Fund-Specific Mode
140	When researching a specific fund:
141	1. Identify the fund's key partners from their website and recent investments
142	2. Map each partner to the closest archetype based on:
143	   - Their career background (founder → Operator, banker → Analyst, VC lifer → Visionary)
144	   - Their public writing and podcast appearances (what topics do they care about?)
145	   - Their portfolio pattern (what types of companies do they invest in?)
146	3. Use the partner's real name but overlay the archetype's evaluation framework
147	4. Note where the real partner diverges from the archetype (e.g., "This partner is primarily an Operator but also has strong thesis-driven conviction, so they may combine Operator and Visionary perspectives")
148	
149	### Assessment Independence
150	Each partner produces their assessment independently before the debate phase. This mirrors real IC dynamics:
151	- Partners prepare their own view before hearing others
152	- The debate surfaces disagreements that wouldn't emerge if everyone just nodded along
153	- A 2-1 split is more informative for the founder than a unanimous rubber stamp
154	
155	### Debate Dynamics
156	After independent assessments, the debate phase has partners respond to each other:
157	- **Agreement amplification** — When two partners agree, they build on each other's reasoning
158	- **Constructive disagreement** — When partners disagree, they challenge each other's assumptions specifically
159	- **Concern escalation** — A concern raised by one partner may be reinforced or dismissed by another
160	- **Synthesis** — The group moves toward consensus, identifying which concerns are dealbreakers vs. addressable

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_016742eNct2Nq1yDjbC426Lr","type":"tool_result","content":"1	# Evaluation Criteria
2	
3	28 dimensions across 7 categories for scoring a startup's IC readiness. Each dimension is evaluated by the agent (LLM) based on available evidence, then scored computationally by `score_dimensions.py`.
4	
5	## Status Values
6	
7	Each dimension receives one of 5 statuses:
8	
9	| Status | Meaning | Score Weight |
10	|--------|---------|-------------|
11	| `strong_conviction` | Clear evidence of strength. Partners would cite this as a reason to invest. | 1.0 |
12	| `moderate_conviction` | Adequate evidence. Not a standout but not a concern either. | 0.5 |
13	| `concern` | Weakness identified. Partners would raise this in discussion. | 0.0 |
14	| `dealbreaker` | Fatal flaw. Any single dealbreaker forces a `hard_pass` verdict. | 0.0 (forces hard_pass) |
15	| `not_applicable` | Dimension doesn't apply to this company's stage or model. | excluded |
16	
17	## Scoring Formula
18	
19	```
20	applicable = count of items where status != "not_applicable"
21	conviction_score = (strong*1.0 + moderate*0.5) / applicable * 100
22	```
23	
24	### Verdicts
25	
26	| Score Range | Verdict | Meaning |
27	|-------------|---------|---------|
28	| >= 75% | `invest` | Strong enough for a term sheet discussion |
29	| >= 50% | `more_diligence` | Promising but needs more evidence on key dimensions |
30	| < 50% | `pass` | Too many concerns to proceed at this time |
31	| any dealbreaker | `hard_pass` | Fatal flaw identified — cannot proceed regardless of score |
32	
33	### Zero-Applicable Edge Case
34	
35	If all 28 dimensions are marked `not_applicable` (or no items provided), the score is `0.0` and the verdict is `more_diligence` with a `ZERO_APPLICABLE_DIMENSIONS` warning. This prevents false positives from empty evaluations.
36	
37	## Categories and Dimensions
38	
39	### Team (4 dimensions)
40	
41	| ID | Dimension | Description |
42	|----|-----------|-------------|
43	| `team_founder_market_fit` | Founder-Market Fit | Do the founders have unique insight, domain expertise, or unfair advantage in this market? Have they lived the problem they're solving? |
44	| `team_complementary_skills` | Complementary Skills | Does the founding team cover the critical bases (technical, commercial, domain)? Are there obvious gaps that need to be filled? |
45	| `team_execution_speed` | Execution Speed | Is the team shipping fast relative to their resources? Evidence of rapid iteration, quick pivots, and bias toward action. |
46	| `team_coachability` | Coachability | Does the founding team take feedback well? Evidence of adapting based on customer/investor/advisor input. Defensiveness is a red flag. |
47	
48	**Stage calibration:**
49	- **Pre-seed:** Founder-market fit and coachability matter most. Team gaps are expected and acceptable.
50	- **Seed:** Complementary skills become important. Solo founders need a plan to build the team.
51	- **Series A:** Full team evaluation. Execution speed must be demonstrated, not just claimed.
52	
53	### Market (4 dimensions)
54	
55	| ID | Dimension | Description |
56	|----|-----------|-------------|
57	| `market_size_credibility` | Size Credibility | Is the stated market size credible and well-sourced? Bottom-up > top-down. Segment-specific > total industry. |
58	| `market_timing` | Timing | Is there a clear macro catalyst (regulatory, technological, behavioral) that makes now the right time? |
59	| `market_growth_trajectory` | Growth Trajectory | Is the market growing, stable, or shrinking? What's the CAGR? Are tailwinds accelerating? |
60	| `market_entry_barriers` | Entry Barriers | How hard is it for new competitors to enter? Regulatory barriers, network effects, switching costs, or technical complexity. |
61	
62	**Stage calibration:**
63	- **Pre-seed:** Market insight matters more than precise sizing. A compelling "why now" can compensate for loose TAM.
64	- **Seed:** Market size should be bottom-up sourced. Timing argument should be concrete.
65	- **Series A:** Market must be large enough for fund-returning outcomes. Growth trajectory must be validated with data.
66	
67	### Product (4 dimensions)
68	
69	| ID | Dimension | Description |
70	|----|-----------|-------------|
71	| `product_differentiation` | Differentiation | What makes this product meaningfully different from alternatives? Feature parity is not differentiation. |
72	| `product_traction_evidence` | Traction Evidence | Concrete proof of product-market fit: revenue, users, engagement metrics, LOIs, waitlist size. Stage-appropriate. |
73	| `product_technical_moat` | Technical Moat | Is there something technically difficult to replicate? Proprietary data, unique architecture, patents, or deep domain-specific engineering. |
74	| `product_user_love` | User Love | Do users/customers actively love the product? NPS, unsolicited referrals, retention data, customer quotes. |
75	
76	**Stage calibration:**
77	- **Pre-seed:** Differentiation and early signal (waitlist, LOIs) suffice. Technical moat can be a plan.
78	- **Seed:** Traction evidence must be concrete (paying customers). User love should be demonstrable.
79	- **Series A:** All four dimensions should show strength. Technical moat must be built, not planned.
80	
81	### Business Model (4 dimensions)
82	
83	| ID | Dimension | Description |
84	|----|-----------|-------------|
85	| `biz_unit_economics` | Unit Economics | Are per-unit economics positive or trending positive? LTV/CAC, contribution margin, payback period. |
86	| `biz_pricing_power` | Pricing Power | Can the company raise prices without losing customers? Evidence of value-based pricing vs. cost-plus. |
87	| `biz_scalability` | Scalability | Does the business model scale without proportional cost increases? Marginal cost of serving the next customer. |
88	| `biz_gross_margins` | Gross Margins | Are gross margins appropriate for the business type? Software: >70%. Services: >40%. Hardware: >30%. |
89	
90	**Stage calibration:**
91	- **Pre-seed:** Business model hypothesis is sufficient. Pricing experiments are a plus.
92	- **Seed:** Unit economics should be emerging. Pricing should be tested with real customers.
93	- **Series A:** Unit economics must be proven and improving. Gross margins should be at or approaching target.
94	
95	### Financials (4 dimensions)
96	
97	| ID | Dimension | Description |
98	|----|-----------|-------------|
99	| `fin_capital_efficiency` | Capital Efficiency | How much value is created per dollar spent? Revenue per dollar raised, headcount efficiency. |
100	| `fin_runway_plan` | Runway Plan | Does current/planned funding provide enough runway to hit milestones for the next round? |
101	| `fin_path_to_next_round` | Path to Next Round | Are the milestones for the next funding round clearly defined and achievable within the runway? |
102	| `fin_revenue_quality` | Revenue Quality | Is revenue recurring, predictable, and diversified? Or lumpy, one-time, and concentrated? |
103	
104	**Stage calibration:**
105	- **Pre-seed:** Capital efficiency is about burn rate discipline. Revenue quality is N/A.
106	- **Seed:** Runway plan should cover 18-24 months. Revenue quality should be emerging.
107	- **Series A:** All financial dimensions should be well-evidenced. Revenue quality is critical.
108	
109	### Risk (4 dimensions)
110	
111	| ID | Dimension | Description |
112	|----|-----------|-------------|
113	| `risk_single_point_failure` | Single Point of Failure | Is the business dependent on one customer, one supplier, one platform, one regulation, or one person? |
114	| `risk_regulatory` | Regulatory Risk | Is the business exposed to regulatory change? How well-prepared is the team for regulatory shifts? |
115	| `risk_competitive_response` | Competitive Response | What happens when incumbents or well-funded startups respond? How defensible is the position? |
116	| `risk_customer_concentration` | Customer Concentration | Is revenue diversified across customers? Top customer <20% of revenue at seed, <10% at Series A. |
117	
118	**Stage calibration:**
119	- **Pre-seed:** Some concentration is expected. Key risk: founder dependency (no team backup).
120	- **Seed:** Concentration should be decreasing. Regulatory awareness should be evident.
121	- **Series A:** No single point of failure should remain unaddressed. Customer diversification is expected.
122	
123	### Fund Fit (4 dimensions)
124	
125	| ID | Dimension | Description |
126	|----|-----------|-------------|
127	| `fit_thesis_alignment` | Thesis Alignment | Does this investment align with the fund's stated investment thesis and focus areas? |
128	| `fit_portfolio_conflict` | Portfolio Conflict | Does the fund already have a conflicting investment? Direct overlap, customer overlap, or adjacent market. |
129	| `fit_stage_match` | Stage Match | Is this company at the right stage for the fund's typical investment? Check size, ownership targets, support model. |
130	| `fit_value_add` | Value-Add Potential | Can the fund add meaningful value beyond capital? Relevant portfolio companies, domain expertise, key relationships. |
131	
132	**Stage calibration:**
133	- Applies equally across all stages
134	- In generic mode: evaluate against a hypothetical early-stage fund thesis
135	- In fund-specific mode: evaluate against the researched fund's actual thesis, portfolio, and focus
136	
137	---
138	
139	## Appendix: SaaS Metrics Reference
140	
141	Canonical formulas and thresholds for SaaS-specific metrics referenced in evaluations. Use these definitions exactly — do not improvise alternative formulas.
142	
143	**If required inputs for a metric are not available from the startup's materials, state this explicitly — do not estimate or assume values.**
144	
145	| Metric | Formula | Key Thresholds | Stage Relevance |
146	|--------|---------|---------------|-----------------|
147	| Magic Number | `(Qtr Rev - Prev Qtr Rev) * 4 / Prev Qtr S&M` | >1.0 efficient, 0.5–1.0 moderate, <0.5 inefficient | Meaningful at Series A with quarterly revenue data. Pre-seed/seed: rarely available, do not require. |
148	| Burn Multiple | `Net Burn / Net New ARR` | <1.5x good, 1.5–2.0x acceptable early, >3.0x red flag | Useful at seed with ARR trajectory. Pre-seed: typically N/A (no ARR). |
149	| Rule of 40 | `Rev Growth % + Profit Margin %` | >40% strong, 20–40% acceptable early, <20% concerning | Series A and later. Pre-seed/seed: growth should dominate; margin is secondary. Note: some firms use "Rule of X" (`Growth % × 2 + FCF Margin %`) which weights growth more heavily — do not substitute without stating which variant is used. |
150	| CAC | `Total S&M / New Customers` | Varies by ACV; break down by channel at Series A | Seed: blended CAC is useful. Series A: channel-level CAC expected. Pre-seed: too early. |
151	| New CAC Ratio | `S&M / New Customer ARR` | <$1.50 good, $1.50–$2.00 acceptable, >$2.00 expensive (2025 median $2.00) | Series A+. Isolates pure acquisition cost from expansion revenue. Use alongside Blended CAC Ratio. |
152	| Blended CAC Ratio | `S&M / (New Customer ARR + Expansion ARR)` | Lower is better; compare to New CAC Ratio to see expansion leverage | Series A+. Shows how expansion revenue amortizes acquisition cost. |
153	| LTV/CAC | `(ARPA × Gross Margin / Churn) / CAC` | >3.0x healthy, <1.0x unsustainable | Seed: directional estimate acceptable. Series A: must be computed with real data. Pre-seed: N/A. |
154	| NDR (Net Dollar Retention) | `(Beg ARR + Expansion - Contraction - Churn) / Beg ARR` | >130% elite, 110–130% good, <100% concerning | Meaningful at seed with 6+ months of cohort data. Series A: expected. Pre-seed: N/A. Always pair with GRR — high NDR can mask high base churn if expansion from a few large accounts dominates. |
155	| GRR (Gross Revenue Retention) | `(Beg ARR - Churn - Contraction) / Beg ARR` | >95% elite, 90–95% strong, 85–90% acceptable, <85% concerning | Same as NDR: meaningful at seed with 6+ months of cohort data. Series A: expected alongside NDR. Pre-seed: N/A. Shows the "leaky bucket" baseline — churn and contraction only, no expansion. |
156	| CAC Payback | `CAC / (ARPA × Gross Margin)` | <12mo excellent, 12–18mo good, >24mo concerning (enterprise ACV may tolerate up to 24mo due to high LTV and low churn) | Seed: useful if data available. Series A: expected. Pre-seed: too early. |
157	| ARR per Employee | `Total ARR / Headcount` | >$150K good early-stage, $200K–$300K+ at scale (AI-native companies often 4–5× higher) | Seed onward as a capital-efficiency signal. Pre-seed: team too small for this to be meaningful. |
158	| Gross Margin | (cross-ref `biz_gross_margins` dimension) | SaaS >70% (top-tier >75%), marketplace >60%, services >40%. AI-native companies may run 25–60% due to inference/infra costs — flag but do not penalize if acknowledged with a path to improvement. | All stages. Pre-seed: target margins acceptable. Seed+: actual margins expected. |
159	
160	---
161	
162	## Appendix: Concern vs. Dealbreaker Thresholds
163	
164	When evaluating a dimension, the boundary between `concern` and `dealbreaker` determines whether the startup gets a "work on this" signal or a hard pass. The following guidance covers the highest-impact dimensions per category.
165	
166	**General rule:** When uncertain, default to `concern`. A dealbreaker is a finding so severe that no amount of strength in other areas can compensate — it makes the investment fundamentally unworkable.
167	
168	| Category | Dimension | Dealbreaker if... |
169	|----------|-----------|-------------------|
170	| **Team** | `team_founder_market_fit` | Founders have zero relevant domain experience AND cannot articulate a credible "why me" — no lived experience, no unfair insight, no relevant network. |
171	| **Team** | `team_coachability` | Founders are actively hostile to feedback or have a documented pattern of ignoring advisor/investor input across multiple interactions. |
172	| **Market** | `market_size_credibility` | The addressable market is provably too small for fund-returning outcomes (e.g., niche with <$100M SAM and no plausible expansion path). |
173	| **Product** | `product_traction_evidence` | At seed+: zero paying customers AND no credible pipeline (LOIs, pilots, waitlist) after 6+ months of effort. Pre-seed: this dimension is rarely a dealbreaker. |
174	| **Business Model** | `biz_unit_economics` | At Series A: unit economics are negative with no improvement trend AND the business model has no structural path to positive unit economics. |
175	| **Financials** | `fin_runway_plan` | Runway is <6 months with no funding pipeline and milestones are unachievable within remaining capital. |
176	| **Risk** | `risk_single_point_failure` | Business depends entirely on a single customer (>80% revenue), single platform (no migration path), or single regulation that is actively under threat. |
177	| **Risk** | `risk_regulatory` | The core business activity is illegal in key target markets or faces imminent regulatory prohibition with no pivot path. |
178	| **Fund Fit** | `fit_portfolio_conflict` | Direct, blocking portfolio conflict — the fund already has an investment in a direct competitor in the same market segment. |

  "verdict": "more_diligence",
  "rationale": "Cadence sits at a genuinely interesting inflection point in a market that has historically been underserved by software. The field service management (FSM) category — plumbers, HVAC techs, landscapers, electricians — represents tens of millions of SMB workers in the US who are still running operations on whiteboards, spreadsheets, and phone calls. The digitization wave that hit retail, restaurants, and professional services is finally arriving for trades and field service, driven by labor shortages pushing owners to squeeze more productivity out of existing crews, and by mobile-first workers who now expect consumer-grade software experiences.\n\nWhat excites me about Cadence is the growth rate: 18% MoM over four consecutive months with 120 paying customers and $40K MRR is not noise — that is genuine pull. At that compounding rate, Cadence is on a trajectory toward $1M ARR within six months. The ex-Stripe, ex-Notion team brings a product philosophy (clean UX, thoughtful systems design) that the incumbents — ServiceTitan, Jobber, HouseCall Pro — have demonstrably failed to deliver for the SMB segment.\n\nHowever, I need more conviction on the 10-year vision before I can say invest. The FSM space has a long history of point-solution products that top out at $50M ARR because they solve scheduling but not the deeper workflow of running a service business: financing, insurance, permitting, customer financing, fleet management. The founders haven't articulated whether Cadence is a workflow system-of-record that expands into adjacent value layers, or just a scheduling tool. That ambition gap — combined with the notable absence of any domain expertise in field service from either founder — keeps me at more_diligence rather than invest. The market timing is right; the vision needs to match it.",
  "conviction_points": [
    "18% MoM growth over four consecutive months at $40K MRR represents genuine product-market pull in a segment (SMB field service) that is actively digitizing: labor scarcity is forcing small operators to adopt scheduling software for the first time, and Cadence's growth rate suggests it is riding this wave rather than pushing against it.",
    "The ex-Stripe + ex-Notion founding profile is a differentiated product bet: Stripe's infrastructure discipline and Notion's PLG design sensibility are precisely the skills needed to build the kind of 'it just works' scheduling tool that trades SMBs will actually adopt — contrasted with ServiceTitan's notoriously complex and expensive product that targets enterprise HVAC and is widely seen as overkill for small operators.",
    "At $1,200 CAC and ~$333/month ARPU with ~80% gross margins, the unit economics are structurally strong for a seed-stage SaaS product. At a 24-month LTV assumption and even modest retention, LTV/CAC exceeds 5x — the kind of ratio that, if it holds at scale, supports a durable and capital-efficient growth engine."
  ],
  "key_concerns": [
    "The FSM category is extraordinarily crowded: the fund's own portfolio contains DispatchPro, ServiceTitan, HouseCall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge, Kickserv, WorkWave, and ReachOut — all direct competitors or adjacent players. Cadence is entering a market where the incumbents are well-capitalized and the category is arguably already in consolidation. The visionary question is not whether Cadence can get to $5M ARR — it probably can — but whether it can reach $100M+ ARR in a market where the top players are already deeply entrenched. How real VC Investment Committees work — structure, decision models, and what kills deals. This reference grounds the IC simulation in actual fund mechanics so the simulation produces realistic, useful feedback.

## What Is an Investment Committee?

The IC is the internal forum where a VC fund decides whether to invest. A partner who has been working with a startup "sponsors" the deal and presents it to the other partners for debate and decision. The founder is not present — this is the conversation that happens behind closed doors.

## Common IC Formats

### The Classic Round Table (Most Common)
- 3-5 partners sit around a table (or video call)
- Sponsoring partner presents (15-20 min)
- Open discussion and Q&A (20-40 min)
- Decision: invest, pass, or request more diligence
- Most seed/Series A funds use this format

### The Memo-First Model
- Sponsoring partner writes a detailed investment memo before the meeting
- Partners read it in advance
- Discussion is focused on disagreements and open questions
- Common at larger, more institutional funds (a16z, Sequoia)

### The Conviction Model
- One partner can champion a deal with strong personal conviction
- IC discussion focuses on "why not" rather than "why"
- Other partners can object but the bar for blocking is higher
- Common at smaller funds where partners have concentrated ownership

## Decision Models

### Unanimous Consent
- All partners must agree to invest
- Any single partner can kill a deal
- Creates conservative portfolio — fewer bets, higher conviction
- Most common at small funds (2-4 partners)

### Majority Vote
- Simple or supermajority (2/3) vote required
- Allows one dissenting partner
- More deals get through, slightly lower average conviction
- Common at larger funds with 5+ partners

### Champion Model
- Sponsoring partner decides, others advise
- IC is a stress-test, not a vote
- Highest throughput but requires deep partner trust
- Common at solo GP funds or very early-stage

## What Happens in the Room

### Phase 1: The Pitch (Sponsor Presents)
The sponsoring partner acts as the founder's advocate. They present:
1. **The opportunity** — market, timing, why this company
2. **The team** — founder-market fit, execution evidence
3. **The business** — traction, unit economics, competitive position
4. **The deal** — terms, round size, who else is in, valuation context
5. **The risks** — honest assessment of what could go wrong
6. **The ask** — how much to invest, at what terms

### Phase 2: The Interrogation
Other partners ask questions. These fall into patterns:
- **Thesis alignment** — "Does this fit what we said we'd invest in?"
- **Competitive landscape** — "Who else is doing this? Why will this team win?"
- **Market reality** — "Is this market as big as presented? What's the real TAM?"
- **Economic viability** — "Do the unit economics work at scale?"
- **Risk assessment** — "What kills this company? What's the single point of failure?"
- **Portfolio fit** — "Do we already have something adjacent? Would this create conflict?"

### Phase 3: The Debate
Partners argue their positions. Common dynamics:
- The **market bull** vs. the **execution skeptic**
- The partner who loves the founder vs. the one who questions the business model
- The "I've seen this movie before" pattern matcher vs. the "this time is different" optimist
- Portfolio construction tension: "We already have X, do we need Y?"

### Phase 4: The Decision
- Explicit decision: invest, pass, or conditional (more diligence needed)
- If invest: terms discussion, ownership target, board seat allocation
- If pass: whether to stay in touch or hard pass
- If more diligence: specific questions/requirements with deadline

## What Kills Deals at IC

### Instant Deal-Killers
1. **Portfolio conflict** — Existing investment in same space, customer overlap
2. **Integrity concerns** — Founder misrepresented data, numbers don't check out
3. **Single point of failure** — Entire business depends on one customer, one regulation, one patent
4. **Adverse reference** — Someone in the network had a negative experience with the founder

### Common Slow Deaths
1. **"Interesting but not now"** — Market timing concerns, no urgency
2. **"Good team, wrong market"** — Impressive founders building in a small or shrinking market
3. **"Math doesn't work"** — Unit economics that require miracles to work at scale
4. **"No moat"** — Nothing preventing a well-funded competitor from copying the approach
5. **"We'd need to see more"** — Traction is promising but not yet convincing for the stage

## Stage-Specific IC Expectations

### Pre-Seed IC
- **Focus:** Team > vision > early signal
- **Key question:** "Are these the founders to solve this problem?"
- **Evidence bar:** Low — conviction is about people and insight, not data
- **Typical deal-killers:** Weak founding team, unclear problem-solution fit, non-differentiated approach

### Seed IC
- **Focus:** Product-market fit signals > team > market
- **Key question:** "Is there evidence that customers want this?"
- **Evidence bar:** Medium — early traction (LOIs, waitlist, pilot revenue), clear ICP, working product
- **Typical deal-killers:** No customer evidence, bloated burn, unfocused GTM

### Series A IC
- **Focus:** Repeatable GTM > unit economics > scale path
- **Key question:** "Can this become a big, efficient business?"
- **Evidence bar:** High — $1M+ ARR, healthy cohorts, repeatable sales motion, clear path to profitability
- **Typical deal-killers:** Leaky cohorts, unclear CAC/LTV, no repeatable sales motion, overpriced round

## How Partners Prepare

Before IC, each partner typically:
1. Reads the investment memo or deal summary
2. Reviews the startup's pitch deck and data room
3. Checks for portfolio conflicts
4. Talks to 1-2 references (customers, industry experts, former colleagues of the founders)
5. Forms an initial view: excited, skeptical, or neutral
6. Prepares 2-3 key questions they want answered in the discussion

## What Founders Should Know

1. **Your sponsor is your advocate** — They've already decided they want to invest. The IC is about convincing the others.
2. **Partners have different lenses** — One cares about market size, another about unit economics, another about team. Address all lenses.
3. **The discussion you don't hear matters most** — What partners say to each other about your startup reveals the real objections. This simulation helps you hear that conversation.
4. **Every concern maps to an action** — A good IC simulation doesn't just identify problems, it shows you what to prepare, what to address proactively, and what to have ready for Q&A.
5. **Consensus is rare** — In real ICs, 2-1 decisions are common. Unanimous enthusiasm is the exception. If the simulation shows some skepticism, that's realistic, not a bad sign.

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01HCrDd9VgAZKt7gijQg7xgE","type":"tool_result","content":"1	# Evaluation Criteria
2	
3	28 dimensions across 7 categories for scoring a startup's IC readiness. Each dimension is evaluated by the agent (LLM) based on available evidence, then scored computationally by `score_dimensions.py`.
4	
5	## Status Values
6	
7	Each dimension receives one of 5 statuses:
8	
9	| Status | Meaning | Score Weight |
10	|--------|---------|-------------|
11	| `strong_conviction` | Clear evidence of strength. Partners would cite this as a reason to invest. | 1.0 |
12	| `moderate_conviction` | Adequate evidence. Not a standout but not a concern either. | 0.5 |
13	| `concern` | Weakness identified. Partners would raise this in discussion. | 0.0 |
14	| `dealbreaker` | Fatal flaw. Any single dealbreaker forces a `hard_pass` verdict. | 0.0 (forces hard_pass) |
15	| `not_applicable` | Dimension doesn't apply to this company's stage or model. | excluded |
16	
17	## Scoring Formula
18	
19	```
20	applicable = count of items where status != "not_applicable"
21	conviction_score = (strong*1.0 + moderate*0.5) / applicable * 100
22	```
23	
24	### Verdicts
25	
26	| Score Range | Verdict | Meaning |
27	|-------------|---------|---------|
28	| >= 75% | `invest` | Strong enough for a term sheet discussion |
29	| >= 50% | `more_diligence` | Promising but needs more evidence on key dimensions |
30	| < 50% | `pass` | Too many concerns to proceed at this time |
31	| any dealbreaker | `hard_pass` | Fatal flaw identified — cannot proceed regardless of score |
32	
33	### Zero-Applicable Edge Case
34	
35	If all 28 dimensions are marked `not_applicable` (or no items provided), the score is `0.0` and the verdict is `more_diligence` with a `ZERO_APPLICABLE_DIMENSIONS` warning. This prevents false positives from empty evaluations.
36	
37	## Categories and Dimensions
38	
39	### Team (4 dimensions)
40	
41	| ID | Dimension | Description |
42	|----|-----------|-------------|
43	| `team_founder_market_fit` | Founder-Market Fit | Do the founders have unique insight, domain expertise, or unfair advantage in this market? Have they lived the problem they're solving? |
44	| `team_complementary_skills` | Complementary Skills | Does the founding team cover the critical bases (technical, commercial, domain)? Are there obvious gaps that need to be filled? |
45	| `team_execution_speed` | Execution Speed | Is the team shipping fast relative to their resources? Evidence of rapid iteration, quick pivots, and bias toward action. |
46	| `team_coachability` | Coachability | Does the founding team take feedback well? Evidence of adapting based on customer/investor/advisor input. Defensiveness is a red flag. |
47	
48	**Stage calibration:**
49	- **Pre-seed:** Founder-market fit and coachability matter most. Team gaps are expected and acceptable.
50	- **Seed:** Complementary skills become important. Solo founders need a plan to build the team.
51	- **Series A:** Full team evaluation. Execution speed must be demonstrated, not just claimed.
52	
53	### Market (4 dimensions)
54	
55	| ID | Dimension | Description |
56	|----|-----------|-------------|
57	| `market_size_credibility` | Size Credibility | Is the stated market size credible and well-sourced? Bottom-up > top-down. Segment-specific > total industry. |
58	| `market_timing` | Timing | Is there a clear macro catalyst (regulatory, technological, behavioral) that makes now the right time? |
59	| `market_growth_trajectory` | Growth Trajectory | Is the market growing, stable, or shrinking? What's the CAGR? Are tailwinds accelerating? |
60	| `market_entry_barriers` | Entry Barriers | How hard is it for new competitors to enter? Regulatory barriers, network effects, switching costs, or technical complexity. |
61	
62	**Stage calibration:**
63	- **Pre-seed:** Market insight matters more than precise sizing. A compelling "why now" can compensate for loose TAM.
64	- **Seed:** Market size should be bottom-up sourced. Timing argument should be concrete.
65	- **Series A:** Market must be large enough for fund-returning outcomes. Growth trajectory must be validated with data.
66	
67	### Product (4 dimensions)
68	
69	| ID | Dimension | Description |
70	|----|-----------|-------------|
71	| `product_differentiation` | Differentiation | What makes this product meaningfully different from alternatives? Feature parity is not differentiation. |
72	| `product_traction_evidence` | Traction Evidence | Concrete proof of product-market fit: revenue, users, engagement metrics, LOIs, waitlist size. Stage-appropriate. |
73	| `product_technical_moat` | Technical Moat | Is there something technically difficult to replicate? Proprietary data, unique architecture, patents, or deep domain-specific engineering. |
74	| `product_user_love` | User Love | Do users/customers actively love the product? NPS, unsolicited referrals, retention data, customer quotes. |
75	
76	**Stage calibration:**
77	- **Pre-seed:** Differentiation and early signal (waitlist, LOIs) suffice. Technical moat can be a plan.
78	- **Seed:** Traction evidence must be concrete (paying customers). User love should be demonstrable.
79	- **Series A:** All four dimensions should show strength. Technical moat must be built, not planned.
80	
81	### Business Model (4 dimensions)
82	
83	| ID | Dimension | Description |
84	|----|-----------|-------------|
85	| `biz_unit_economics` | Unit Economics | Are per-unit economics positive or trending positive? LTV/CAC, contribution margin, payback period. |
86	| `biz_pricing_power` | Pricing Power | Can the company raise prices without losing customers? Evidence of value-based pricing vs. cost-plus. |
87	| `biz_scalability` | Scalability | Does the business model scale without proportional cost increases? Marginal cost of serving the next customer. |
88	| `biz_gross_margins` | Gross Margins | Are gross margins appropriate for the business type? Software: >70%. Services: >40%. Hardware: >30%. |
89	
90	**Stage calibration:**
91	- **Pre-seed:** Business model hypothesis is sufficient. Pricing experiments are a plus.
92	- **Seed:** Unit economics should be emerging. Pricing should be tested with real customers.
93	- **Series A:** Unit economics must be proven and improving. Gross margins should be at or approaching target.
94	
95	### Financials (4 dimensions)
96	
97	| ID | Dimension | Description |
98	|----|-----------|-------------|
99	| `fin_capital_efficiency` | Capital Efficiency | How much value is created per dollar spent? Revenue per dollar raised, headcount efficiency. |
100	| `fin_runway_plan` | Runway Plan | Does current/planned funding provide enough runway to hit milestones for the next round? |
101	| `fin_path_to_next_round` | Path to Next Round | Are the milestones for the next funding round clearly defined and achievable within the runway? |
102	| `fin_revenue_quality` | Revenue Quality | Is revenue recurring, predictable, and diversified? Or lumpy, one-time, and concentrated? |
103	
104	**Stage calibration:**
105	- **Pre-seed:** Capital efficiency is about burn rate discipline. Revenue quality is N/A.
106	- **Seed:** Runway plan should cover 18-24 months. Revenue quality should be emerging.
107	- **Series A:** All financial dimensions should be well-evidenced. Revenue quality is critical.
108	
109	### Risk (4 dimensions)
110	
111	| ID | Dimension | Description |
112	|----|-----------|-------------|
113	| `risk_single_point_failure` | Single Point of Failure | Is the business dependent on one customer, one supplier, one platform, one regulation, or one person? |
114	| `risk_regulatory` | Regulatory Risk | Is the business exposed to regulatory change? How well-prepared is the team for regulatory shifts? |
115	| `risk_competitive_response` | Competitive Response | What happens when incumbents or well-funded startups respond? How defensible is the position? |
116	| `risk_customer_concentration` | Customer Concentration | Is revenue diversified across customers? Top customer <20% of revenue at seed, <10% at Series A. |
117	
118	**Stage calibration:**
119	- **Pre-seed:** Some concentration is expected. Key risk: founder dependency (no team backup).
120	- **Seed:** Concentration should be decreasing. Regulatory awareness should be evident.
121	- **Series A:** No single point of failure should remain unaddressed. Customer diversification is expected.
122	
123	### Fund Fit (4 dimensions)
124	
125	| ID | Dimension | Description |
126	|----|-----------|-------------|
127	| `fit_thesis_alignment` | Thesis Alignment | Does this investment align with the fund's stated investment thesis and focus areas? |
128	| `fit_portfolio_conflict` | Portfolio Conflict | Does the fund already have a conflicting investment? Direct overlap, customer overlap, or adjacent market. |
129	| `fit_stage_match` | Stage Match | Is this company at the right stage for the fund's typical investment? Check size, ownership targets, support model. |
130	| `fit_value_add` | Value-Add Potential | Can the fund add meaningful value beyond capital? Relevant portfolio companies, domain expertise, key relationships. |
131	
132	**Stage calibration:**
133	- Applies equally across all stages
134	- In generic mode: evaluate against a hypothetical early-stage fund thesis
135	- In fund-specific mode: evaluate against the researched fund's actual thesis, portfolio, and focus

139	## Appendix: SaaS Metrics Reference
140	
141	Canonical formulas and thresholds for SaaS-specific metrics referenced in evaluations. Use these definitions exactly — do not improvise alternative formulas.
142	
143	**If required inputs for a metric are not available from the startup's materials, state this explicitly — do not estimate or assume values.**
144	
145	| Metric | Formula | Key Thresholds | Stage Relevance |
146	|--------|---------|---------------|-----------------|
147	| Magic Number | `(Qtr Rev - Prev Qtr Rev) * 4 / Prev Qtr S&M` | >1.0 efficient, 0.5–1.0 moderate, <0.5 inefficient | Meaningful at Series A with quarterly revenue data. Pre-seed/seed: rarely available, do not require. |
148	| Burn Multiple | `Net Burn / Net New ARR` | <1.5x good, 1.5–2.0x acceptable early, >3.0x red flag | Useful at seed with ARR trajectory. Pre-seed: typically N/A (no ARR). |
149	| Rule of 40 | `Rev Growth % + Profit Margin %` | >40% strong, 20–40% acceptable early, <20% concerning | Series A and later. Pre-seed/seed: growth should dominate; margin is secondary. Note: some firms use "Rule of X" (`Growth % × 2 + FCF Margin %`) which weights growth more heavily — do not substitute without stating which variant is used. |
150	| CAC | `Total S&M / New Customers` | Varies by ACV; break down by channel at Series A | Seed: blended CAC is useful. Series A: channel-level CAC expected. Pre-seed: too early. |
151	| New CAC Ratio | `S&M / New Customer ARR` | <$1.50 good, $1.50–$2.00 acceptable, >$2.00 expensive (2025 median $2.00) | Series A+. Isolates pure acquisition cost from expansion revenue. Use alongside Blended CAC Ratio. |
152	| Blended CAC Ratio | `S&M / (New Customer ARR + Expansion ARR)` | Lower is better; compare to New CAC Ratio to see expansion leverage | Series A+. Shows how expansion revenue amortizes acquisition cost. |
153	| LTV/CAC | `(ARPA × Gross Margin / Churn) / CAC` | >3.0x healthy, <1.0x unsustainable | Seed: directional estimate acceptable. Series A: must be computed with real data. Pre-seed: N/A. |
154	| NDR (Net Dollar Retention) | `(Beg ARR + Expansion - Contraction - Churn) / Beg ARR` | >130% elite, 110–130% good, <100% concerning | Meaningful at seed with 6+ months of cohort data. Series A: expected. Pre-seed: N/A. Always pair with GRR — high NDR can mask high base churn if expansion from a few large accounts dominates. |
155	| GRR (Gross Revenue Retention) | `(Beg ARR - Churn - Contraction) / Beg ARR` | >95% elite, 90–95% strong, 85–90% acceptable, <85% concerning | Same as NDR: meaningful at seed with 6+ months of cohort data. Series A: expected alongside NDR. Pre-seed: N/A. Shows the "leaky bucket" baseline — churn and contraction only, no expansion. |
156	| CAC Payback | `CAC / (ARPA × Gross Margin)` | <12mo excellent, 12–18mo good, >24mo concerning (enterprise ACV may tolerate up to 24mo due to high LTV and low churn) | Seed: useful if data available. Series A: expected. Pre-seed: too early. |
157	| ARR per Employee | `Total ARR / Headcount` | >$150K good early-stage, $200K–$300K+ at scale (AI-native companies often 4–5× higher) | Seed onward as a capital-efficiency signal. Pre-seed: team too small for this to be meaningful. |
158	| Gross Margin | (cross-ref `biz_gross_margins` dimension) | SaaS >70% (top-tier >75%), marketplace >60%, services >40%. AI-native companies may run 25–60% due to inference/infra costs — flag but do not penalize if acknowledged with a path to improvement. | All stages. Pre-seed: target margins acceptable. Seed+: actual margins expected. |

162	## Appendix: Concern vs. Dealbreaker Thresholds
163	
164	When evaluating a dimension, the boundary between `concern` and `dealbreaker` determines whether the startup gets a "work on this" signal or a hard pass. The following guidance covers the highest-impact dimensions per category.
165	
166	**General rule:** When uncertain, default to `concern`. A dealbreaker is a finding so severe that no amount of strength in other areas can compensate — it makes the investment fundamentally unworkable.
167	
168	| Category | Dimension | Dealbreaker if... |
169	|----------|-----------|-------------------|
170	| **Team** | `team_founder_market_fit` | Founders have zero relevant domain experience AND cannot articulate a credible "why me" — no lived experience, no unfair insight, no relevant network. |
171	| **Team** | `team_coachability` | Founders are actively hostile to feedback or have a documented pattern of ignoring advisor/investor input across multiple interactions. |
172	| **Market** | `market_size_credibility` | The addressable market is provably too small for fund-returning outcomes (e.g., niche with <$100M SAM and no plausible expansion path). |
173	| **Product** | `product_traction_evidence` | At seed+: zero paying customers AND no credible pipeline (LOIs, pilots, waitlist) after 6+ months of effort. Pre-seed: this dimension is rarely a dealbreaker. |
174	| **Business Model** | `biz_unit_economics` | At Series A: unit economics are negative with no improvement trend AND the business model has no structural path to positive unit economics. |
175	| **Financials** | `fin_runway_plan` | Runway is <6 months with no funding pipeline and milestones are unachievable within remaining capital. |
176	| **Risk** | `risk_single_point_failure` | Business depends entirely on a single customer (>80% revenue), single platform (no migration path), or single regulation that is actively under threat. |
177	| **Risk** | `risk_regulatory` | The core business activity is illegal in key target markets or faces imminent regulatory prohibition with no pivot path. |
178	| **Fund Fit** | `fit_portfolio_conflict` | Direct, blocking portfolio conflict — the fund already has an investment in a direct competitor in the same market segment. |

### What Cadence Gets Right

Two dimensions scored strong conviction, and the overall conviction score of 32.1 with 14 moderate-conviction dimensions tells an important story: there is a real business here. The 18% month-over-month growth from a $480K ARR base is genuinely impressive — that trajectory, sustained, gets you to Series A territory in under 18 months. Partners in this IC recognized the growth signal and did not dismiss it. The complementary founding team (payments infrastructure + PLG product design) shows real craft in building products that SMBs actually adopt.

These are strengths to lead with in every investor meeting. When a partner asks "why are you winning customers?", your answer needs to be precise: which specific customers, what made them switch, and what do they say when they refer you to a peer.
